>> I think this is a wonderful question and
I think the answer is fascinating and it
starts with a long slow process that
begins around the medieval period. But
before we get to that we got to get to
what the commandment actually is. And
the commandment is found in Exodus 20:7.
And in the Hebrew, it literally says to
not lift, bear, or carry the name of
Adonai, your God in vain. And scholars
are in pretty widespread agreement that
the point here is to prohibit the
invocation of God's name in the swearing
of an oath that is either a lie or that
one does not intend to keep. And we have
a parallel commandment in Leviticus
19:12 that is a little more explicit
where God says,"Do not swear by or using
my name for a lie." And so the idea here
seems to be don't use my name. Don't
invoke my name in swearing an oath that
is insincere. That is a lie. Whether it
is an oath in a courtroom where you're
saying I didn't steal the thing or an
oath where you're saying by the life of
Adonai I will do this thing. Now a
couple of interesting things happen
after the composition of these
prohibitions.
One is a taboo develops on pronouncing
God's name outside of very specific
circumstances in the temple. And so this
commandment takes on a new significance
where you're not supposed to invoke
God's name at all in public because that
would be profane. Profane comes from a
Latin word profanom which means outside
the temple. And then we have the
destruction of the temple which means
that every place becomes outside of the
temple. So the taboo becomes
universalized. You're just not supposed
to invoke God's name. Now another thing
develops and this is the notion that to
lift, bear or carry the name refers to
representing God through the community
where you are a representative of God's
people and in that sense you lift bear
or carry the name. So this is the
interpretation that you're not supposed
to do bad things as a representative of
God. So this is a very very old
interpretation. It's not what the
commandment was originally intended to
prohibit, but it is a very, very early
interpretation.
Now, we've got to fast forward a bit to
late antiquity giving way to the
medieval period. And here we've got this
prohibition on swearing oaths by God's
name. Now, in public, a lot of people
are pushing back against that taboo by
swearing in God's name or using the word
God in oaths. An example from outside of
the Christian community would be by
Odin's beard, where we have a lot of
exclamations that sound like they are
the invocation of the name for God in an
oath. And here's an example that is
given in a wonderful book on the history
of swearing from 2011. And you can see
they got pretty creative up to and
including using little replacements for
the word god. So they might say cod or
they might say gad or they might say cog
or something else entirely as a way to
kind of buck the taboo while also not
technically bucking the taboo.
And because you have people pushing back
against the taboo, you also have
religious leaders pushing it back
against the push back. And you get the
development of the moralization of
public speech where you're supposed to
speak in proper ways in public. And then
you have another development in this
category of swearing. So swearing has
primarily a religious dimension. To
swear is to swear an oath invoking words

appropriate context. But then you also

the moralization of speech and the
developing taboss is the use of

today. They have reference more to

the religious dimension. So swearing
becomes multi-dimensional. The religious
dimension is one side of it, but you
also have this other side of it. And
both of these become ways to push back
against the moralization of speech. But
we still have this understanding of the
commandment as uh a reference to
representing God's people uh by bearing,

member of that community. And this has
to do with communalism. You're
representing your community. But as we
move into the early modern and the
modern period, we get a lot more
individualism. So that becomes less
salient. And what becomes more salient
is this notion that you're supposed to
speak appropriately in public. That
comes to the four. And there's another
reason that this comes to the four. Not
only is individualism taking over
communalism, but we're also beginning to
see this become a bit of costly
signaling. In proper society, you're
expected to do certain things as a way
to signal to other members of the
society that you can be trusted, that
you're one of the good ones. And both of
the interpretations of this commandment
can function as costly signaling. But
the it means don't swear interpretation
is one that comes up a lot more
regularly, is one that's a lot easier to
recognize, and is one that's a lot
easier to police. And so as a means of
boundary maintenance and as a means of
policing people's behavior in public,
it's a lot easier if we understand this
commandment, one of the main ten
commandments to mean don't say oh my
god, don't use God's name in public.
Don't swear oaths that invoke words for
deity. So that becomes a much more
useful tool for people who are trying to
engage in boundary maintenance and for
people who are trying to engage in
credibility enhancing displays. And
that's where you amplify the costly
signals as a way to say I'm willing to
go above and beyond the lowest common
denominator when it comes to costly
signaling. And so that interpretation
becomes much more useful to identity
politics. And as Christianity becomes
more about identity politics, the
interpretation of this commandment as
don't swear an oath using a name for God
becomes the most prominent
interpretation. The other interpretation
is much less common, is much harder to
